name: Edith Cooper
bio: Poet, born 1862, the younger half of "Michael Field" and the niece of her collaborator and life partner Katharine Bradley (1846-1914). "Michael Field" is not a person but the single joint pen name under which Bradley and Cooper published everything: eight volumes of poetry, some twenty-seven verse dramas, and a joint diary, Works and Days. Wilde addressed his letters to "Michael Field", writing to the pair as one correspondent. On the Y90s account Cooper was the more retiring and fragile of the two and tended to follow her aunt's lead; in the diary's private mythology she was "Field", Henry, or the Persian Puss. Evangelista notes that despite the two women's constant devotion to each other Cooper was prone to heterosexual infatuations, including a period of attachment to their friend Bernhard Berenson. She died of cancer in 1913; Bradley followed within the year.
bio_note: Dates (1862-1913) from the editors' identifying footnote to Wilde's letter to "Michael Field", Complete Letters (2000), p. 449, read at the rendered page image 2026-08-03, and corroborated in Evangelista's Y90s biography of Michael Field (2015).

sources.quote: Dear Michael Field, Write to Miss Elisabeth Marbury, c/o Low's Exchange, New York City, USA. She manages all my plays. I have written to her. I am a wretch not to have answered sooner, but I have no excuse; so you will forgive me. Your third act was quite admirable - a really fine piece of work - with that touch of terror our stage lacks so much. I think the theatre should belong to the Furies. Caliban and Silenus, one educated and the other sober, seem now to dominate, in their fallen condition, our wretched English drama. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to 'Michael Field', [? late October 1893], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. He is helping them place a play in America and praising their third act. The Caliban and Silenus line is Wilde on the contemporary English stage.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde acting for them professionally, and what he thought of their play.
